questions.stem: A light ray meets a flat mirror, making an angle of 30° with the mirror surface. At what angle to the normal is it reflected?
questions.explanation: Angles of incidence and reflection are measured from the normal, the line perpendicular to the mirror. A ray at 30° to the surface is at 60° to the normal, so it reflects at 60°. Giving 30° uses the angle to the surface.

questions.stem: Which describes the image of an object formed by a plane mirror?
options: Real, inverted, the same size, and as far behind the mirror as the object is in front
Virtual, upright, smaller, and closer to the mirror than the object is in front
Real, upright, the same size, and formed on the surface of the mirror itself
Virtual, upright, the same size, and as far behind the mirror as the object is in front
questions.explanation: Reflected rays appear to come from a point behind the mirror, but no light actually goes there, so the image is virtual. It is upright, the same size and the same distance behind the mirror as the object is in front, and it is laterally inverted.

questions.stem: On a diagram of a wave, how are rays drawn compared with wavefronts?
options: Rays join the troughs of the wave and are drawn half a wavelength apart
Rays are drawn at 45° to the wavefronts and show the wave's amplitude
Rays are perpendicular to the wavefronts and show the direction of travel
Rays are parallel to the wavefronts and show the positions of the crests
questions.explanation: A wavefront joins points in the same phase, such as a line of crests, and a ray shows the direction the wave travels, which is always at right angles to the wavefronts. Wavefronts are spaced one wavelength apart.

questions.stem: What causes light to refract as it passes from air into glass at an angle?
options: Its speed changes as it crosses the boundary
Its frequency changes as it crosses the boundary
It reflects partly off the glass surface
Its amplitude falls as the glass absorbs it
questions.explanation: Refraction happens because a wave's speed changes at the boundary between two media. The part of a wavefront that enters first changes speed first, so the wavefront turns. The frequency is set by the source and does not change.

questions.stem: Straight water waves pass at an angle from deep water into shallow water, where they travel more slowly. What happens to the waves?
options: Their wavelength decreases and they bend towards the normal
Their frequency decreases and they bend towards the normal
Their wavelength increases and they bend away from the normal
Their wavelength decreases and they bend away from the normal
questions.explanation: The frequency is unchanged, so slower waves have a shorter wavelength (v = fλ). The wavefronts close up and turn so that the waves bend towards the normal, just as light does entering a medium where it travels more slowly.

questions.stem: Light travels at 2.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ in a type of glass. Using c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, what is the refractive index of the glass?
questions.explanation: n = c/v = 3.00 × 10⁸/2.0 × 10⁸ = 1.5. Dividing v by c gives 0.67, but a refractive index is never less than 1, since nothing travels faster than light in a vacuum.

questions.stem: Water has a refractive index of 1.33. Using c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, what is the speed of light in water?
questions.explanation: v = c/n = 3.00 × 10⁸/1.33 ≈ 2.26 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. Multiplying by n gives a speed greater than c, which is impossible, and c itself is the speed only in a vacuum.

questions.stem: Light passes from air into glass, which has a higher refractive index. What happens to its speed and direction?
options: It speeds up and bends away from the normal
It slows down and bends towards the normal
It speeds up and bends towards the normal
It slows down and bends away from the normal
questions.explanation: A higher refractive index means a lower speed (v = c/n). By Snell's law, n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂, so a larger n₂ gives a smaller θ₂: the ray bends towards the normal.

questions.stem: A ray of light passes from air (n = 1.00) into glass (n = 1.50) with an angle of incidence of 40°. What is the angle of refraction?
questions.explanation: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂ gives sin θ₂ = 1.00 × sin 40°/1.50 = 0.429, so θ₂ ≈ 25°. Multiplying by 1.50 instead of dividing gives sin θ₂ = 0.964 and 75°, which would mean bending away from the normal.

questions.stem: A ray of light passes from water (n = 1.33) into air (n = 1.00) with an angle of incidence of 30°. What is the angle of refraction?
questions.explanation: sin θ₂ = n₁ sin θ₁/n₂ = 1.33 × 0.500/1.00 = 0.665, so θ₂ ≈ 42°. Light going into a medium of lower index bends away from the normal. Dividing by 1.33 gives 22°, which bends the wrong way.

questions.stem: Light passes from a medium with refractive index 1.2 into one with refractive index 1.6. What is the ratio of its speed in the second medium to its speed in the first?
questions.explanation: Since v = c/n, v₂/v₁ = n₁/n₂ = 1.2/1.6 = 0.75: light is slower in the medium of higher index. Taking n₂/n₁ gives 1.33, which would mean it speeds up.

questions.stem: For light meeting a boundary between two transparent media, which pair of conditions produces total internal reflection?
options: Light travels towards a medium of lower refractive index, at less than the critical angle
Light travels towards a medium of higher refractive index, at less than the critical angle
Light travels towards a medium of lower refractive index, at more than the critical angle
Light travels towards a medium of higher refractive index, at more than the critical angle
questions.explanation: Total internal reflection can only happen when light is trying to pass into a medium where it would travel faster (lower n), because only then does it bend away from the normal. If the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle, no refracted ray exists and all the light reflects.

questions.stem: What is the critical angle for light travelling from glass (n = 1.50) into air (n = 1.00)?
questions.explanation: sin θ_c = n₂/n₁ = 1.00/1.50 = 0.667, so θ_c ≈ 42°. At this angle of incidence the refracted ray would travel along the surface. Giving 48° confuses the critical angle with its complement.

questions.stem: What is the critical angle for light travelling from glass (n = 1.50) into water (n = 1.33)?
questions.explanation: sin θ_c = n₂/n₁ = 1.33/1.50 = 0.887, so θ_c ≈ 62°. This is larger than the 42° for glass to air because the indices are closer together. Using air's index gives 42°, and 49° is the critical angle for water to air.

questions.stem: In an optical fibre, why must the core have a higher refractive index than the cladding around it?
options: So light striking the core-cladding boundary beyond the critical angle is totally internally reflected
So light speeds up in the core and reaches the far end before it can leak out through the cladding
So light refracts into the cladding and is guided along the outside of the fibre to the far end
So light is absorbed less in the core because a higher index makes the glass more transparent
questions.explanation: Total internal reflection needs light to be travelling towards a medium of lower refractive index. A higher-index core lets light that strikes the boundary at more than the critical angle reflect again and again along the fibre. Light is actually slower in the higher-index core.

questions.stem: To find the refractive index of a glass block, a student plots sin θ in air against sin θ in glass for several rays. The gradient is 1.48 and the accepted value is 1.50. What are the measured index and its percentage error?
options: 1.50, with a percentage error of 1.3%
1.48, with a percentage error of 1.3%
0.68, with a percentage error of 55%
1.48, with a percentage error of 2.0%
questions.explanation: With air's index taken as 1.00, sin θ_air = n sin θ_glass, so the gradient is n = 1.48. The percentage error is |1.48 − 1.50|/1.50 × 100 ≈ 1.3%. The value 0.68 is the reciprocal of the gradient.

questions.stem: Why is a refractive index found from the gradient of a graph of sin θ₁ against sin θ₂ more reliable than a value from a single ray?
options: Plotting a graph removes all systematic errors, such as a protractor that is misaligned by 2°
The gradient is always exactly equal to the accepted value, whatever the size of the errors
A single ray cannot be refracted, so a graph is the only way to measure a refractive index
The line of best fit through many points reduces the effect of random errors in individual readings
questions.explanation: Each angle reading carries random error. Fitting a line through many readings averages these out, and outliers become easy to spot. A graph does not remove a systematic error, which shifts every reading the same way.

questions.stem: A short-sighted person sees nearby objects clearly but distant objects are blurred. Where does the eye focus light from distant objects, and which lens corrects this?
options: Behind the retina; a diverging (concave) lens
In front of the retina; a diverging (concave) lens
Behind the retina; a converging (convex) lens
In front of the retina; a converging (convex) lens
questions.explanation: In short-sightedness (myopia) the eye bends light too strongly, so distant objects focus in front of the retina. A diverging lens spreads the rays a little before they enter the eye, moving the focus back onto the retina.

questions.stem: A long-sighted person cannot focus clearly on nearby objects. Which describes the problem and its correction?
options: Light from near objects focuses in front of the retina; a diverging lens reduces the bending
Light from near objects would focus behind the retina; a diverging lens adds the extra bending
Light from near objects focuses in front of the retina; a converging lens reduces the bending
Light from near objects would focus behind the retina; a converging lens adds the extra bending
questions.explanation: In long-sightedness (hyperopia) the eye does not bend light enough, so light from near objects would come to a focus behind the retina. A converging (convex) lens starts bending the rays inward before they reach the eye, bringing the focus forward onto the retina.

questions.stem: When is the diffraction of a wave through a gap most noticeable?
options: When the gap is much larger than the wavelength
When the wave has a very large amplitude
When the wave travels faster than usual
When the gap is about the same size as the wavelength
questions.explanation: Waves spread out most when the opening is similar in size to their wavelength. Through a gap many wavelengths wide, the waves pass through with only a little spreading at the edges.

questions.stem: You can hear someone talking in the next room through an open doorway, but you cannot see them. What best explains this?
options: Sound wavelengths are similar to the doorway's width, so sound diffracts; light wavelengths are far smaller
Sound waves travel faster than light waves, so sound reaches you around the corner before the light does
Light wavelengths are similar to the doorway's width, so light diffracts so much it becomes too faint to see
Sound is a transverse wave and can diffract, while light is longitudinal and can only travel in straight lines
questions.explanation: Speech has wavelengths from several centimetres to a few metres, similar to a doorway's width, so it spreads strongly around the edges. Visible light has wavelengths around 500 nm, about a million times smaller than the doorway, so it barely diffracts. Light is much faster than sound, and it is the transverse one.

questions.stem: When water waves diffract through a gap in a harbour wall, what happens to their wavelength and speed?
options: The wavelength decreases and the speed decreases
The wavelength increases and the speed stays the same
The wavelength stays the same and the speed increases
Both stay the same; only the direction of travel spreads out
questions.explanation: Diffraction changes the shape and direction of the wavefronts, not the medium, so the speed and frequency are unchanged, and therefore so is the wavelength. A change of speed and wavelength is what happens in refraction.

questions.stem: Two pulses on a rope travel towards each other. One has a displacement of +3 cm and the other −1 cm. What is the displacement where they fully overlap?
options: +2 cm
+4 cm
−2 cm
+3 cm
questions.explanation: By the principle of superposition, the resultant displacement is the sum of the individual displacements: +3 + (−1) = +2 cm. The pulses then pass through each other unchanged. Adding the sizes gives 4 cm, which ignores the opposite signs.

questions.stem: When does constructive interference occur at a point where waves from two identical sources meet?
options: When the waves arrive out of phase, with a path difference of half a wavelength
When the waves arrive in phase, with a path difference of half a wavelength
When the waves arrive out of phase, with a path difference of a whole number of wavelengths
When the waves arrive in phase, with a path difference of a whole number of wavelengths
questions.explanation: If the path difference is 0, λ, 2λ and so on, crests meet crests and troughs meet troughs, so the displacements add to give a maximum. A path difference of half a wavelength (or 1.5λ and so on) brings crests onto troughs, causing destructive interference.

questions.stem: Two speakers emit the same 340 Hz tone in phase, and sound travels at 340 m s⁻¹. Point P is 3.0 m from one speaker and 3.5 m from the other. What is heard at P?
options: A loud sound, because the path difference is a whole wavelength
A quiet sound, because the path difference is a whole wavelength
A quiet sound, because the path difference is half a wavelength
A loud sound, because the path difference is half a wavelength
questions.explanation: The wavelength is 340/340 = 1.0 m, so the path difference of 0.5 m is half a wavelength. Compressions from one speaker arrive with rarefactions from the other, and destructive interference gives a minimum.

questions.stem: A student walks slowly along a line in front of two speakers playing the same tone in phase. What does she hear, and why?
options: Alternating loud and quiet regions, as the path difference changes between whole and half wavelengths
A steady sound everywhere, as the two waves add together in the same way at all points
A sound that gets steadily louder, as she moves closer to the midpoint between the speakers
Alternating high and low pitches, as the frequency changes along the line between maxima
questions.explanation: As she moves, the difference in her distance from the two speakers changes. Where it is a whole number of wavelengths the waves interfere constructively (loud); where it is an odd number of half-wavelengths they interfere destructively (quiet). The frequency, and so the pitch, does not change.

questions.stem: How is a standing wave formed on a string fixed at both ends?
options: Two waves of different frequency travel in the same direction
A single wave stops moving when it reaches a fixed end
A wave diffracts as it passes over the fixed ends
Two identical waves travelling in opposite directions superpose
questions.explanation: A wave reflected from the fixed end travels back and superposes with the incoming wave of the same frequency and amplitude. Their superposition gives a pattern of nodes and antinodes that does not travel along the string.

questions.stem: What is a node in a standing wave?
options: A point that oscillates with the largest amplitude because of constructive interference
A point where the wave reflects and changes into a longitudinal wave
A point that moves along the string at the speed of the travelling waves
A point that stays at zero displacement because of destructive interference
questions.explanation: At a node the two travelling waves always cancel, so the string there does not move. Antinodes are the points midway between nodes where the waves reinforce, giving the largest oscillation.

questions.stem: What is the distance between two adjacent nodes in a standing wave?
options: A quarter of a wavelength
Two wavelengths
Half a wavelength
One wavelength
questions.explanation: Adjacent nodes are half a wavelength apart, and a node and the next antinode are a quarter of a wavelength apart. This is why the fundamental on a string of length L has λ = 2L.

questions.stem: A guitar string 0.80 m long is fixed at both ends, and waves travel along it at 240 m s⁻¹. What is the frequency of its fundamental (first harmonic)?
options: 300 Hz
75 Hz
192 Hz
150 Hz
questions.explanation: The fundamental has one loop, with nodes at the two ends, so λ = 2L = 1.6 m. Then f = v/λ = 240/1.6 = 150 Hz. Taking λ = L gives 300 Hz, which is the second harmonic.

questions.stem: The string 0.80 m long with a wave speed of 240 m s⁻¹ vibrates with three antinodes. What are the wavelength and frequency of this standing wave?
options: 1.6 m and 150 Hz
2.4 m and 100 Hz
0.27 m and 900 Hz
0.53 m and 450 Hz
questions.explanation: Three antinodes means three half-wavelengths fit the string: 3(λ/2) = 0.80, so λ ≈ 0.53 m and f = 240/0.533 = 450 Hz, three times the fundamental. Multiplying the length by 3 instead gives 2.4 m and 100 Hz.

questions.stem: A string 1.2 m long, fixed at both ends, vibrates at 200 Hz in a standing wave with four loops. What is the speed of the travelling waves on the string?
options: 120 m s⁻¹
240 m s⁻¹
60 m s⁻¹
960 m s⁻¹
questions.explanation: Each loop is half a wavelength, so 4(λ/2) = 1.2 m and λ = 0.60 m. Then v = fλ = 200 × 0.60 = 120 m s⁻¹. Treating each loop as a whole wavelength gives λ = 0.30 m and 60 m s⁻¹.

questions.stem: An ambulance with its siren on drives towards you and then away. What do you hear?
options: A lower pitch as it approaches and a higher pitch as it moves away
A higher pitch as it approaches and the true pitch as it moves away
The same pitch throughout, but louder as it approaches and quieter after
A higher pitch as it approaches and a lower pitch as it moves away
questions.explanation: As the source approaches, the waves ahead of it are bunched up, so a higher frequency reaches you. As it recedes they are spread out and the frequency is lower. The siren itself emits the same frequency throughout.

questions.stem: A car horn of frequency 500 Hz moves at 20 m s⁻¹ directly towards a stationary listener. The speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹. What frequency does the listener hear?
options: 531 Hz
472 Hz
529 Hz
500 Hz
questions.explanation: Using f′ = f(v_wave + v_observer)/(v_wave − v_source) with the observer at rest: f′ = 500 × 340/(340 − 20) ≈ 531 Hz. Using 360 in the denominator treats the source as moving away (472 Hz), and 529 Hz is what an observer moving at 20 m s⁻¹ towards a stationary source would hear.

questions.stem: The 500 Hz horn now moves at 20 m s⁻¹ directly away from the stationary listener. The speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹. What frequency does the listener hear?
options: 472 Hz
531 Hz
471 Hz
480 Hz
questions.explanation: For a receding source the source velocity counts as negative in f′ = f(v_wave + v_observer)/(v_wave − v_source), so f′ = 500 × 340/(340 + 20) ≈ 472 Hz. The value 531 Hz is for the source approaching, and 471 Hz is what a listener moving away from a stationary source would hear.

questions.stem: A cyclist rides at 10 m s⁻¹ directly towards a stationary 400 Hz siren. The speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹. What frequency does she hear?
options: 410 Hz
412 Hz
388 Hz
400 Hz
questions.explanation: With the observer moving towards the source, f′ = f(v_wave + v_observer)/v_wave = 400 × 350/340 ≈ 412 Hz. Subtracting her speed gives 388 Hz, the frequency heard while riding away. Simply adding 10 to the frequency gives 410 Hz.

questions.stem: The spectral lines in light from a distant galaxy are shifted towards the red end of the spectrum. What does this show?
options: The galaxy is moving away from us
The galaxy is moving towards us
The galaxy is very hot
The galaxy is spinning rapidly
questions.explanation: When a light source moves away, the waves reaching us are stretched to longer wavelengths, a redshift. A source moving towards us shows a blueshift, to shorter wavelengths. Temperature affects which colours are emitted, not the positions of the lines.

questions.stem: A spectral line emitted at 656 nm is observed at 660 nm in the light from a star. What can be concluded?
options: The star is moving closer, because the observed frequency is lower than the emitted one
The star is moving away, because the observed wavelength is longer than the emitted one
The star is moving closer, because the observed wavelength is longer than the emitted one
The star is moving away, because the observed frequency is higher than the emitted one
questions.explanation: A longer observed wavelength, and so a lower observed frequency, is a redshift, which means the source is receding. A source moving closer would show a shorter wavelength and higher frequency, a blueshift.
